accuracy.evidence: Rhyme is defined as a shared rime from the last stressed vowel onward, as in Goswami and Bryant's account of onset and rime and the Oxford English Dictionary sense of rhyme (correspondence of terminal sounds). Every pair was checked by ear and against standard British and American pronunciations: hat, bat, rat with cat (/æt/); bee, tree; frog, log; cake, snake; fox, box; bread, sled, red with bed (/ɛd/); bear, chair (/ɛə/ or /ɛr/ in both accents); goat, boat; honey, money (/ʌni/); kitten, mitten; flower, tower (/aʊə/). Distractors were checked not to rhyme: car, cup, dog, bus, fish, kite, duck, bell, web, hammer, hungry, goal, gate, bean. The adult text says rhyme awareness is an early step in phonological awareness without overclaiming that it causes reading success.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented confusions in early rhyme judgement (alliteration taken as rhyme, near misses, spelling-led judgements and meaning-led choices, noted in Bryant, Bradley and colleagues' oddity tasks and in Development Matters guidance): same start (car and cup on the cat train, sun and sock in p3 and the challenge), close but different end (bell and web in step 3, p5, the bed challenge, goal in m7), letters over sound (bear and chair in step 4, m3, challenge 'spell'), linked meaning (kitten and cat in the challenge and m8), and matching the start of long words (honey and hammer in step 5, m4).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagrhyme is about judging and finding rhyme by ear: a cat train that only accepts words with the same end sound and rejects same-start words, an oddity task in four sets, a near-miss board around bed, rhyme spotting at the ends of poem lines, and two-beat rhyme pairing with a same-start decoy. flagrime builds words from onset and rime tiles and families, and flagbyheart is about memorising a song; neither has near-miss rejection, line-end rhyme spotting or two-syllable rhymes. lab_distinct gate passes under 30%.

lab_teaches.evidence: Children find the rule before the text gives it: car and cup bounce off the train with a message that compares the ends, the odd-one-out feedback names the shared end, bell is turned away while bread, sled and red go green, tapping big or brown in the poem says that a same start is not a rhyme, and hammer is left over because it only starts like honey. Every tapped word is spoken aloud where the device has speech, so it is an ear task, not a reading task.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with tempting wrong options the lab disproves: 'Yes, they start the same' for cat and cup (cup is turned away), 'Yes, it sounds very close' for bell and bed (bell is rejected while red rhymes), and 'No, the letters are different' for bear and chair (the poem shows they rhyme).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions, each wrong option tagged with one of five distinct messages: same start is not a rhyme, close but the very end differs, rhyme is sound not letters, same meaning is not rhyme, and being short or in the same list is not rhyme. Answer order rotates between questions.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use one- and two-syllable words and short sentences with the words said out loud (c-at, h-at); the adult text names CCSS RF.K.2.a, the Year 1 programme of study wording, the EYFS Development Matters statement and key terms. Canvas labels are a few words, all task words are spoken on tap, and the lab uses the young layout with big cards and buttons. validate_lessons readability passes.

no_filler.evidence: Filler gate clean. Each kid paragraph adds one idea: what rhyme is, same start and near misses, sound not letters, rhymes in poems and long words. Items mix choosing a rhyme (p1, p4, m1, m4, m7), rejecting a same start (p3), near misses (p5), the odd one out (m2), spelling (m3), the rule (m6), pairs (m8), poem line ends (m9) and counting rhyme words (p2, m5).

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 light, 360 px Android dark and desktop light and dark screenshots of every step at the start and after Show me. At 360 px the cat train shows cat plus three seats and six large picture cards in a 3 by 2 grid with readable names; the bed board fits five cards in two rows; poem words are chips at least 33 px tall; the long-word columns keep 4 cards on the right without clipping. Real mouse drags onto the train and between the long-word columns were tested and complete the tasks.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin with the picture and the word: put each word on the cat train, pick the odd one out, ask whether each word rhymes with bed, every poem word by line and position, and pick then pair a long word. The canvas aria-label is rewritten after each action with why a word does or does not rhyme. walk.cjs axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
